To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the antigenic drift in influenza A viruses can be detected by serologic assays and that reference antigens or antisera need to constantly be replaced to keep pace with antigenic drift.
antigenic differences among influenza A viruses (H5N2 subtype) are influenced by the antigen and the antiserum used in the hemagglutation inhibition (HI) assay.
antigenic and genetic changes in influenza viruses can significantly affect the results of serosurveillance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an improved strategy for the serologic surveillance and control of AI viruses in poultry and swine farms.
the impact of antigenic and genotypic drift of AI viruses in Mexico.
the development of new methods for serologic surveillance of AI viruses in order to reduce the risk of introduction of new AI viruses and the emergence of novel pandemic strains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the HI test is an appropriate method for serosurveillance but the reference antigens/antisera need to be updated periodically.
serosurveys should be performed with antigens and antisera that are as similar as possible to the viruses that are circulating.

the antigenic drift of the hemagglutinins of the H5N2 LPAI viruses circulating in Mexico between 2002 and 2008 was not sufficient to cause serological discrepancies between reference antiseras and field isolates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
antigenic and genetic differences between circulating AI virus and vaccine strains can be underestimated when using standard HI assay and reference reagents.

the antigenic differences between influenza virus field isolates and vaccine strains should be determined using HI assays with reference antigens and/or antibodies that are closely related to circulating virus.

the serological surveillance of influenza viruses in poultry and pigs should include the use of a panel of antigens (or antisera) representative of circulating viruses to improve the accuracy of serosurveillance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the antigenic and genetic characteristics of influenza A viruses are constantly changing, and the use of reference antigens and antisera for serologic surveillance of AI viruses must be constantly updated to ensure accurate results.
the HI test is an excellent tool to detect antigenic changes in AI viruses.
serosurveys of AI viruses need to be constantly updated to reflect the genetic and antigenic changes of circulating viruses.
